(2) A forward (generative) model of transition dynamics, P(st+k∣st,at:t+k)P(s_{t+k} \mid s_t, a_{t:t+k}).

Empowerment is defined over the actuator-sensor channel, which means the agent must possess an internal model that predicts how the sensory state will change as a function of actions emitted from the current state. This is the same generative/forward model required by EFE minimization and model-based planning more broadly, but empowerment places a specific demand on its interventional fidelity: the model must accurately capture how outcomes differentially change across the full action repertoire, not merely predict the most likely next state under a default policy. In causal-inference terms, empowerment requires a model of P(s′∣do(a),s)P(s' \mid \mathrm{do}(a), s)–an interventional distribution–rather than the merely observational P(s′∣s)P(s' \mid s) that suffices for passive prediction 1. In realistic partially observed settings, this requirement lifts to the agent’s inferred state: the forward model must propagate a latent/belief representation (e.g., P(zt+1∣zt,at)P(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,a_t) with an observation model P(ot∣zt)P(o_t\mid z_t), or directly P(bt+k∣bt,at:t+k)P(b_{t+k}\mid b_t,a_{t:t+k})), since controllability estimates are otherwise confounded by hidden variables and perceptual aliasing 2. For the multi-step case (k>1k>1), this all requires either an explicit kk-step rollout through the transition model (compounding approximation errors at each step 3) or a learned "jumpy" model that directly predicts P(st+k∣st,at:t+k)P(s_{t+k} \mid s_t, a_{t:t+k}) without intermediate unrolling–a substantial function-approximation challenge given the exponential growth of the action-sequence space.

Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior?

The brain implements action-conditional forward models at multiple hierarchical levels, with architecturally distinct systems covering different temporal horizons and abstraction scales. At the fastest timescale, the cerebellum functions as a dedicated forward model for sensorimotor dynamics, acquiring paired inverse-forward controller modules (learned as internal models of limb/plant dynamics) that predict the sensory consequences of motor commands on the order of tens to hundreds of milliseconds 4, 5. Critically, the interventional character demanded by empowerment–prediction under do(a) rather than passive observation–is secured by the efference copy / corollary discharge architecture: motor commands routed to the periphery simultaneously send an efference copy to predictive circuits (via cerebellum, thalamus, and sensory cortex), allowing the system to distinguish self-caused from externally caused state changes and thereby maintain a genuinely action-indexed transition model 6. This wiring is an evolutionary architectural prior–corollary discharge pathways are phylogenetically ancient, identifiable in invertebrates and conserved across vertebrate taxa 6–meaning that the brain does not need to learn that actions have causal consequences on sensory input; only the specific parameters of those consequences require experience-dependent calibration.

For longer-horizon, more abstract forward modelling, the hippocampal-entorhinal system and prefrontal cortex jointly support multi-step rollout through mental simulation. Hippocampal "preplay" and replay sequences sweep through place- and concept-cell assemblies in compressed time, effectively unrolling candidate action trajectories through a learned cognitive map of state space 7, 8, while prefrontal networks maintain and evaluate the predicted outcomes of these trajectories in working memory. The hippocampal system naturally operates over latent/belief representations rather than raw sensory input–place cells, grid cells, and object-vector cells encode allocentric spatial and relational structure abstracted away from immediate sensory particulars 9, 10–satisfying the requirement for forward modeling over inferred states P(zt+1∣zt,at)P(z_{t+1}∣z_t,a_t). Evolutionarily, the entorhinal-hippocampal loop architecture, the fixed theta-phase organization that temporally structures look-ahead sequences 11, and the grid-cell lattice geometry itself 12 all constitute architectural priors that scaffold rapid acquisition of structured world models without specifying their content. The brain thus addresses the multi-step rollout problem not through a single mechanism but via a hierarchy: fast, precise cerebellar forward models for immediate sensorimotor consequences, and hippocampal-prefrontal simulation for more abstract, temporally extended (k>>1) action-contingent prediction–with evidence suggesting that the latter may also learn "jumpy" abstractions at the level of temporally extended options or subgoals rather than exclusively performing step-by-step unrolling 13, 14.
